research_concepts: defensive suppression of opponent second-half change
regression to the mean in half-to-half change
methodological_questions: Is the opponent H2-H1 change attributable to a defense stable across split halves of a season and across adjacent seasons?
How much true between-team variance exists relative to sampling noise with 120 team-seasons (about 30 teams over 4 seasons)?
Can the mechanical H1-level to H2-change dependence (RTM), opponent quality, garbage time and score state be removed from the trait?
What permutation or placebo baseline shows the trait is not noise or a re-labelling of overall defensive quality?

historical_evidence.finding: H1 usage of a play type as a predictor of H2 suppression was a powered null once H1 PPP / mean reversion was controlled (all BH-adjusted tests null or WEAK). Predictive lift over the mean-reversion baseline was +0.039 (0.550 vs 0.511). The record says the bulk of H2 suppression is RTM. n=8873 team-games.

For the variance of H1->H2 PPP collapse, H1 PPP alone (RTM) explained 32.9%. Usage, process/shot-zone, lineup and context added about 1.7 pp in total, and 65.4% was unexplained, which the record attributes to idiosyncratic noise from small per-half n.

A different team-level trait question (structural concentration vs defensive vulnerability, n=117, 30 franchises) gave a CI spanning 0 (rho=+0.079, CI [-0.114,+0.234]). The record calls this a powered null.

Descriptive sweep of opponent-relative defensive edges over 870 ordered pairs. The record notes the edges depend only on the defense (e.g. DAL PNR +9.2% for every offense), so they are not matchup-specific.
Equilibrium and actual-mix matchup predictors had negative R2, while the team-offense mean had R2 +0.1197. Opponent-strength scaling made R2 worse.

Inferred within-game and cross-game defensive scheme-change labels could not separate real adjustment from the offense executing differently. The transition matrices were near-uniform, consistent with label noise.
The adapt-vs-continue matched-pair comparison rested on a post-hoc reconstructed cohort. The Group B CI included 0 (n=255 pairs).
Descriptive halftime, crunch and post-run play-type mix shifts only. The record notes the OTHER label is noisy.
Team AVOID% ranged from 50.6% to 6.8% in H2 trigger games. The record gives no outcome test and notes small player samples.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Predicting H2 suppression from H1 play-type reliance beyond mean reversion
failed_approaches.why: RTM_SELECTION: most of the apparent suppression is regression to the mean; lift over baseline is tiny and does not survive BH.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Explaining H1->H2 PPP collapse with process, usage, lineup and context variables
failed_approaches.why: Powered null: RTM accounts for about 95% of what was explained, and the residual is small-per-half-n noise.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Inferring defensive scheme change from derived play-type labels
failed_approaches.why: Label or classification error: the labels cannot separate defense from offense execution.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Post-hoc adapt vs continue cohort comparison
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as untestable with RISK:PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE and RISK:SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER; the cohort is not a validated adaptation sample.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Matchup-specific model predictors (equilibrium, actual-mix, opponent-strength lambda)
failed_approaches.why: Negative R2, worse than the simple team mean (powered null).

evidence_establishes: In this project's earlier work, half-to-half change in PPP is dominated by regression to the mean, and process, usage, lineup and context variables add very little (FAM:SF-APPS-070, FAM:SF-APPS-076).

Team-level simple means have been more predictive than richer matchup models (FAM:SF-APPA-020), and defensive edges have been defense-specific rather than matchup-specific (FAM:SF-APPA-034, descriptive only).
evidence_does_not_establish: Nothing retrieved directly tests whether a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is stable across split halves of a season or across seasons.
Nothing retrieved estimates between-team variance components or an ICC for H2-H1 change.
The nulls were on play-type usage and suppression-trigger framings, not on a team-level defense random-effect framing, so they do not directly reject it.
Retrieved team-level work used a different outcome and 30 franchises.
own_inferences: Per-game H2-H1 PPP differences are very noisy, so a team-season mean over about 85 games probably has a standard error larger than any plausible true between-defense SD. I expect low split-half reliability.

If the raw opponent H2-H1 change is used, it will probably correlate with defense quality and opponent H1 level through RTM and give an artifactually positive stability. The estimand must therefore be residualized, and the residual probably carries little stable signal.
A stable defensive trait, if present, could be real or could be a proxy for pace, bench depth, coaching tendencies or opposing schedule. Reliability alone would not show it is a defensive adjustment.

The 120 team-seasons give about 90 adjacent-season pairs (and fewer independent team clusters), so the test can only detect moderate stability (about r>=0.3). It can rule out large stability but not small.
uncertainties: Number of games, possessions and playoff share per team-season in each file is not stated.
It is unknown whether garbage-time and score-state filters are feasible with the supplied fields; they likely are via play-by-play score and clock.
Roster and coach turnover between seasons will attenuate cross-season stability, so cross-season correlations understate a true within-roster trait.
The 120 team-seasons presumably cover 4 seasons x 30 teams, but this is not confirmed. It is unclear whether playoff team-seasons are included in or beyond that count.
The effect of 2025-26 data versioning is not recorded.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history the decision would likely have been a straightforward reliability analysis. The retrieved RTM-dominated nulls (FAM:SF-APPS-070, FAM:SF-APPS-076) moved me toward requiring residualization against the opponent's H1 level and a permutation placebo, and toward a low prior of finding a reliable trait. The records did not test this question directly, so they did not move the decision to do_not_proceed.

blocking_constraints.text: Only about 120 team-seasons and about 90 adjacent-season pairs; the test can resolve reliability of roughly 0.3 or more and cannot resolve small true stability.
Opponent H2-H1 change is mechanically tied to the opponent's H1 level; without residualization the estimand is dominated by RTM.

prior_work.summary: Earlier work shows H1->H2 PPP change is mostly RTM and that usage, lineup and context add almost nothing (powered nulls on adjacent framings). A team-level reliability test of a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change was not retrieved, so the specific question is not directly answered.

risks.text: Mechanical negative dependence of H2-H1 change on H1 level. Residualize on opponent H1 PPP (or an out-of-sample opponent expectation), and use H1-based opponent level estimated from other games only.
Per-half possession counts are small, so game-level H2-H1 differences are very noisy. Use possession-weighted estimators and report reliability with CIs.
Defense quality, opponent quality, home/away, rest, pace and blowout/garbage-time substitution patterns can create a stable team-level signal that is not a defensive adjustment effect.
About 30 team clusters per season, repeated across seasons, so adjacent-season pairs are not independent; CIs must be clustered by team.
Rosters, coaches and league scoring environment change across seasons, attenuating cross-season stability.
The apparent trait must exceed a permutation baseline where opponents' defense labels are shuffled within season and game-date.
Multiple outcome definitions (PPP, points, eFG), filters and reliability metrics inflate false positives unless one is designated primary.
Opponent expectations must not use the same game or future games of the target team-season; use leave-one-game-out or prior-games means.

design.estimand: Defense effect D(t,s) = possession-weighted mean over team t's games in season s of [opponent H2 PPP minus opponent H1 PPP] minus the expected change given the opponent's H1 PPP and opponent-season baseline (RTM-adjusted residual, expected value from a model fit on all other games). Trait reliability = (a) split-half correlation of D with Spearman-Brown correction (odd/even games, 1000 random splits), and (b) correlation of D across adjacent seasons for the same franchise, plus ICC from a mixed model with team and team-season random intercepts.
design.unit: Team-season (defense side), with game-level residuals as the underlying observations.
design.sample: All 120 team-seasons, 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular seasons (data as of 2026-10-06). Primary analysis is regular season only; playoffs are a secondary, separately reported analysis because of the very small per-team samples. Exclusions pre-specified: possessions after the point when the margin is 20 or more with under 6 minutes left in H2 (garbage time), overtime, and games with fewer than 40 possessions per half.
design.power: About 85 games per team-season. If the per-game residual SD is about 0.25 PPP, the team-season SE is about 0.03 PPP. With 90 adjacent-season pairs, the SE of r is about 0.10, so the minimum detectable cross-season r is about 0.28 at 80% power. A pre-registered power simulation using observed per-game residual variance will fix the minimum detectable true-trait SD before unblinding outcomes.
design.controls: Opponent H1 PPP (computed from other games), opponent season-average H2-H1 change, home/away, rest days, pace, H1 margin, defense's own H1 quality (opponent H1 PPP allowed relative to league), and starter-minutes share in H2. Sensitivity analyses: with and without garbage-time filter, and with the defense's overall quality partialled out of D.
design.falsification: Permutation placebo: shuffle defense labels among opponents within season and game-date (5000 permutations) and recompute split-half and cross-season reliability; observed reliability must exceed the 97.5th percentile of the permuted distribution. Second placebo: replace the H2-H1 residual with a random half-split of games, which should give no stable signal. Also verify that the unadjusted statistic shows a spurious stability that disappears after RTM adjustment.
design.multiplicity: One primary statistic: cross-season correlation of D (PPP basis). Secondary: split-half reliability, ICC, and playoff analysis, with Holm correction across those three. Alternative outcome definitions are exploratory and labelled as such.
design.decision_rule: Supported if cross-season r >= 0.20 with the 95% team-clustered bootstrap lower bound > 0, split-half Spearman-Brown >= 0.30, and both exceed the permutation 97.5th percentile after Holm. Rejected (no reliable trait) if the 95% upper bound of cross-season r < 0.25 and the split-half upper bound < 0.35. Otherwise inconclusive. If the effect appears only before RTM adjustment, report as artifact.
design.data_version: Per-game NBA stats API files and derived play-by-play data as of 2026-10-06, with 2025-26 regular season and playoffs treated as complete. Freeze the extracted dataset and its hash before analysis, and fix filters and the model specification in the pre-registration.

research_concepts: defensive suppression of opponent second-half adjustment
split-half and season-to-season stability of defensive effect
regression to the mean in half-to-half change
methodological_questions: Is a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change a stable, reliable team trait across seasons or split halves?
How much between-team variance in H2-H1 change remains after accounting for sampling noise with about 120 team-seasons?
How should opponent quality, score state, garbage time, and mechanical regression to the mean be controlled?
What placebo or permutation baselines are needed to show the trait is not noise?
args.query: reliability of team defensive effect on opponents' second-half minus first-half change, team-season stability, intraclass correlation, split-half, regression to the mean

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- search_documents(query): rank further study-family documents by text relevance; returns up to 10 families not yet returned.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm going to wrap up with the final answer now, sticking closely to the records and statuses that were actually returned. The analysis covers 120 team-seasons (30 teams across 4 seasons, including 2025-26), and the question comes down to whether a defense's effect on opponents' second-half-minus-first-half change is a stable team trait, with split-half reliability and season-to-season ICC as the ways to check that. Regression to the mean looks like it's driving much of the pattern, with APPS-070 and APPS-076 as the main cases to point to.

I'm estimating how reliable a team's defensive effect would be, using the expected per-game noise to judge whether a stable trait could even be detected. I'm leaning toward a rejection as most likely, with the pre-set threshold in mind, and the historical statuses stand as returned: APPS-070 and APPS-076 rejected, APPA-005 and APPS-025 untestable, APPS-015 and APPM-021 not hypothesis tests, and PAP-024 rejected.

I'm now setting out the study design: freezing the data as of 2026-10-06 across the four completed seasons, defining each defense's effect as the residual change in opponents' per-possession scoring from the first half to the second, adjusted for regression to the mean. Reliability will be checked two ways, split-half by odd and even games within a season with Spearman-Brown correction, and season-to-season across adjacent pairs using a mixed model for the variance components, with a placebo test to follow.

I'm now spelling out the validation rules: a permutation test that shuffles opponents' defense labels within each date and season, plus repeat runs using only first-half and only second-half levels. I'm also adding controls for the main confounder, since good defenses suppress opponents' first-half scoring and that can inflate the second-half change through regression to the mean, along with coaching, rotations, margin, rest, and home court.

I'm settling on the output format now, a compact JSON structure that covers the design, thresholds, and the historical statuses already returned.
